This is nothing new, especially for the bottom 50%. The real disposable incomes of the poorer half of Americans have stagnated or shrunk significantly over the last several decades. Trump's reckless actions ensured that many more people have fallen on hard times more recently.

Based on the history of this country for the past forty-or-so years--I hate to say it, but: the idea of elected officials as a major part of our solution to our human existential and physical exhaustion is not promising, nor helpful.

Instead, our American democratic system has proven itself to be vulnerable and beholden to the big money that runs most of what has occurred in our lives since the 1980s. 

Since its inception, this country's congressional makeup, even most state and local governments are completely run by and for overt monied interests of corporations--those very businesses whose practices damage society and the environment because of the "pro" corporate stance as taken by regulatory agencies within government.

Corporate "bottom-line" thinking brings about a sense of exhaustion in the populace as we live with the reality of this thinking. 

 It's "exhausting" to not make enough money to live safely or decently after working to put in a 12-hour day; demoralization is rampant when corporations are polluting water, land, and air, or daily are damaging, killing, destroying habitat just so big profits can keep a plethora of their business-friendly candidates running and winning and staying in office.

Constant tension is simple to begin a cure for:
revolutionize the political reality in this nation away from monied abuse and successes by instead getting regular people to run for office themselves effecting a meaningful stewardship toward major policy change.

comments.name: Karen
comments.body:
My partner died of cancer at home. His doctor told him about a week before he passed there was nothing else that could be done for him, and asked if he wanted hospice care. I had told him that when that time came, he would need to answer. He did. We waited days and hospice failed to come. I called the doctor's office and demanded the on-call doc call me. When he did, I asked if my dear was dying. He answered, but he was wrong - Rich was a fighter and didn't want to die. I also told the doc hospice had not called or come. 2 nights later Rich had a pain emergency and I fed him liquid morphine until he could rest. That morning he was lucid but very weak. Hospice came that day and he died that night, unconscious from the meds they gave him. We didn't get to say goodbye, but I was lying next to him when he took his last breath. His doctor AND hospice failed him and me. This was in 2007, in the SF East Bay. 
I think there should be no shame regardless of where a person dies. Death is personal - the individual dying is the one who does it and no one else can change that - the best they can do is try to be there for them in the way they can accept. 
Now I have lost 2 partners to death. The 2nd was worse and he passed alone in the hospital, which still makes my want to jump out of my skin. Both my parents died alone, and that too still makes me sad. I hope that is not my fate.
It is good to hear that some hospitals have units where people can die in soft light and quiet.

comments.name: Annie
comments.body: Twenty years ago my mother died from metastatic bladder cancer. It was her wish to die at home, under hospice care. I was her primary caregiver, but had a lot of help from family members. Even then, it took a huge emotional and physical toll on me. Toward the end, when she was unable to communicate, I'd wonder, is she in pain, is she hot or cold, can she hear me? And then afterwards, I'd wonder, did I do everything right? I'm glad we were able to give Mom the home care she wanted until the end. But I have decided I don't want to put that responsibility on my daughter when my time comes.

comments.name: FP
comments.body: Thank you for this much needed perspective. My mother died from complications of breast cancer and was in home hospice. As her primary caretaker, it was absolutely exhausting and hard on our entire family and the expectation was that we would somehow soldier on till the end. My mother’s last 48 hours was not easy and was not a good death. Home hospice fills some of the gaps but not nearly enough. Looking back, I wish my mom had passed away in a hospital room under the care of nurses and doctor’s that could have managed her symptoms and brought her pain under control. By the time my mother passed, I felt shell shocked and out of my mind with exhaustion. I couldn’t even properly say goodbye to the most important person in my life.

comments.name: Ceilidth
comments.body:
Our daughter died of breast cancer in the hospital.  On her next to the last day, she asked to go to the hospital.  She was planning to become a hospice patient within the week but she was feeling very sick and wanted the help that a hospital could provide.  None of us realized that she was at the very end of her life when she went there.  She went from the ER to a room and over half a day it was clear that this was where she would die.  There were no massive interventions but there was a tremendous amount of care and caring and pain management.  She died peacefully in the hospital.  Frankly I am glad she did not die at home.  What the nurses were able to provide for her and for us was a level of comfort care she would never have had at home because neither her husband or us, her parents, could have done what the nurses did.  

Dying at home can be the best way to go.  My mother was a long term hospice patient and died at home.  She woke up one morning, asked for a cup of coffee, tried to sit up and her heart stopped.  But not everyone dies like that.  These days, home hospice provides much less actual help with care than she got and, most of the people whom I know whose life ended recently with hospice care died, not at home, but in a hospice facility often in a hospital and I believe were charged separately for that facility.

comments.name: Mel
comments.body:
@Daniela J. Lamas, my father was sent home from the hospital for in-home hospice care. He was riddled with cancer, and it was a miserable few days. He was in pain, enraged, delirious, and clearly needed more medication. The hospice provider took hours to respond to calls, barely medicated him, sent prescriptions to pharmacies that didn't deliver them, and it took 3 days for one of the hospice nurses to finally say it was unmanageable at home, after he became very agitated in front of her. It wasn't enough that in his pain and delirium, he repeatedly shouted and physically lashed out at us. She arranged for a hospice center, and he was finally properly medicated and out of pain. But the in-home experience was dreadful, and 7 years later, I still vividly recall his rage, which was directed at my sibling and me. 
By contrast, my husband died in the hospital following a failed AAA surgery. The hospital (and hospice providers) kept trying to send him home, and his surgeon fought for him to stay in the hospital. I am forever grateful for that surgeon. It wasn't an easy environment, but the care was quite good, and he didn't suffer.

comments.name: Tim
comments.body: As a hospice medical director, I think the author is missing the use of General Inpatient Status (GIP in Medicare Hospice terminology) which allows a patient with uncontrolled symptoms not only to remain in a hospital setting and receive intravenous medication for pain, breathlessness while still receiving the benefits of hospice.   Remember, hospice benefits the entire family of the patient, with over a year of bereavement support for families after a loved one dies.   When someone dies in the ICU without hospice, there is little or none of this follow on support.   Hospice can be done on an inpatient setting - it’s a key caveat that was left out in this essay

comments.name: SarrisFerniwick
comments.body:
In Costuming class in college, I learned that before men wore Great Coats (1600s?) ALL garments buttoned as women's clothing currently button (right over left). The Great Coat was the first overgarment worn OVER a man's sword (which was decoratively worn by men who never intended to duel or go to battle). Buttons were reversed on the Great Coat in order to reach in, right handed, and pull out a sword that was under the coat.
Rather than maintain 2 buttoning directions for men, all clothing shifted to left over right for men. As a costumer, it is important to know this because historical costumes for men earlier than the time of the Great Coat must button right over left to be historically accurate. 
This is not a myth. Look at historical clothing. Before the Great Coat, men's clothing buttoned right over left, and women's clothing, even for those who were of a class that dressed themselves always buttoned right over left.

comments.name: Kevin
comments.body:
I would disagree. Writing is very important. Pretty much everybody is going to deal with contracts at some point, for example; one's ability to work with written text is essential for that. Or maybe you need to write a letter to a company or an elected official, or even to someone you know (friend, family, potential spouse—remember love letters?). To be persuasive, convincing, poignant, or even just entertaining, it helps to know how to write.

The more important point here is that we spend almost no time learning how to debate. Consequently, most of us are lacking in the ability to craft a coherent argument on any given topic, so when we are challenged we tend to become defensive or aggressive. Anyone who has talked with someone who shut down further discussion the topic with "well, that's my opinion" surely recognizes this. If our schools taught us how to have rational debates about topics we disagree on, we might still have more of the civility most of us consider to have disappeared long ago.

comments.name: Michael
comments.body:
Like many others in the comment section, I, too, am a college professor. There is certainly value in a discussion where teachers prompt students, students build off each others’ thoughts, and the group can arrive at a new understanding of a novel, poem, image, or idea. I use discussion every class session as a way for students to give their ideas a test run in a low-stakes environment. Producing a final, polished product is the end result of this process. Whether that end product is a video essay, an analytic essay, a presentation-students should work towards something that they can take pride in creating. 

One issue that is not addressed in this essay is the ethics of asking students to use AI to augment their final product. Using AI is not an ethically neutral pedagogical practice. It uses water, it uses electricity, and it makes routine the extraction of knowledge for a few.

comments.name: Paul
comments.body: It's true that listening and speaking extemporaneously are important skills. One benefit of the written word, both in reading and writing, is that it stays put, it doesn't vanish into thin air as soon as it is spoken, or when class is dismissed.  Writing allows precise reflection on specific aspects of an argument, and that reflection can happen days or weeks or months or years after the argument is made.  Thoughts and speech are airy, and writing is thinking made into sold form - offering a different kind of utility from what we gather through listening and speaking.  Both are needed, equally.

comments.name: Dandelion
comments.body: Actually, writing skills are crucial in arts & humanities. As an art historian, I've had to edit publications collecting research papers written by multiple scholars. Scholars who never bothered to learn grammar tend to write the way they speak. Too many sentences in their papers, as written, carry  ambiguous meanings. It takes forever, and a lot of diplomacy, to edit their written work so that it actually communicates what they're trying to say.

comments.name: Lee
comments.body:
You aren't wrong. In my classroom, I'm moving a lot more towards emphasizing real-time knowledge making and synthesis. Writing isn't EVERYTHING.

But I still can't shake the feeling that we're seeing a rush of academics trying to excuse AI and to metabolize it into a new pedagogy for the expressed purpose of carving out a niche for themselves in whatever academy comes next.

comments.name: S
comments.body: The value of dialog in the practice of critical thinking is not to be underestimated, I agree. It's essential, and dialog facilitation skills are critical teaching skills, agreed. So, too, the value of carefully created human written expression in its varied forms, is not to be dismissed lightly from the curricula. Does AI really force us to choose between improvisation and composition? They're both important and merit time in the academy. Students can often reach such conclusions in the course of discussing the stuff and encountering written and spoken words on the subject. I teach in a college, too.

comments.name: Charles
comments.body:
My PhD orals were difficult because I’d never been tested by face-to-face speech throughout my entire university career: it was all written essays, written tests.

Writing can be edited before submission; speech rarely is. We blurt out our thoughts whatever they may be — sometimes to deep regret. Writing and editing help expunge our errors of expression.

I’m a writer; I like writing. It helps me look smarter than I actually am.

comments.name: Illinois English Professor
comments.body:
Surely the author errs in claiming that "most college professors" believe that students learn to think ONLY by writing. I doubt any of my faculty colleagues (including those of us who teach writing) would make such a claim.

And yes, conversation among minds is a powerful stimulant to thought, but it seems self-evident that writing (as well as speaking) can facilitate such conversation.   See the comments on the op-ed, for example.

I don’t trust most books published after 2022. I know that it’s cool to use AI, but, for what? The information isn’t always real and the authors can’t always be bothered to write themselves.

comments.name: James Dodge MD
comments.body:
Great investigative journalism by students, BUT… 

The article in The Dartmouth (newspaper) reads like a “Got ‘cha” piece unless it is appreciated that the job of a student and the jobs of non students are not the same. 

Having a single standard of what is and what is not acceptable for all is the wrong approach and we are poorly served by trying to pretend otherwise. 

We are truly living on the AI frontier and in retrospect some uses will be considered inappropriate by wherever we eventually draw the line between appropriate and inappropriate, but (going meta here) that does not mean that works generated prior to the line being drawn were appropriate or inappropriate. The exploration of all the possible ways to incorporate AI are necessary for us to determine where that future drawn line will be. ￼

I applaud Dartmouth (the college) for embracing the role of academic institutions in exploring this new frontier and working to settle this new field to the benefit of the many stakeholders trying to learn and work in an unfamiliar land. 

(No portion of the above was written with AI — I’m not sure whether I should be sorry or not with this admission, but I guess that is just an example of the frontier life we are all living.)

comments.name: Metaphor
comments.body:
I am a retired faculty member. I remember when administrators informed departments that they had to develop "assessment" tools. I asked, "what is 'assessment'?" I never got a straight answer, so I went along with the game and made up some sort of gobbledygook assessment "tools" for my courses. To this day I still don't understand what is the whole point of "assessment."

If I were still teaching I am pretty sure my administration would tell me that I had to become proficient in AI. As with assessment, my response would be to feign compliance while I went ahead and did things the old-fashioned way, which is to say, to rely on my own intelligence and think for myself.

comments.name: DTS
comments.body: I am genuinely interested to learn how my engineering student are using AI in work I assign (which I prepare and grade the old fashioned way), so I ask them (in a neutral manner) to describe their use of AI for building spreadsheets, coding, writing and editing, etc. while reminding them they are responsible for all their work. In a period of transition, I feel this is the most realistic way for me to grow as an educator of real world students. Part of my growth is also tied to learning about and teaching the real world environmental and cognitive consequences of using these tools.

comments.name: Bethany Winslow
comments.body: There are different purposes for different kinds of writing tasks, and we can't just lump everything together as if its all equivalent. For college students, much of the writing expected of them has been used as evidence of their critical thinking and synthesis skills. It's how they've been asked to demonstrate what they've learned. They'll earn a grade that is supposed to represent that they've achieved a learning goal. But not all writing needs to do that. If I was in marketing and selling a product, I wouldn't care who wrote the marketing copy that works the best the task. The purpose of many writing tasks are simply to convey information, and do so in the most expedient manner.   College professors might need to remix their own materials to make a new course, an updated lecture, or a redesigned assignment, so AI tools would allow them to do that quickly. Their task in that moment is to get the right information into a format that suits their teaching purpose. It could be an alternative explainer of a course concept or a synthesis of a department's request. Either way, those written artifacts are not being submitted as evidence they've done the hard work of thinking or synthesis. That's not the point of that work. We take the end product that has their name attached to it which means they've told us the information is accurate and that they stand by it. An important aspect of critical thinking is understanding nuance.  Authorship in the age of AI is a nuanced challenge.

comments.name: W.B.
comments.body:
The sooner we accept that the teacher is going to be replaced with a robot the easier it will be to digest the issues here. 

Look, kids are going to cheat. The robot teacher will to the rote and boring work of explaining to them why they are being required to use their own brains. 

The robot teacher will deliver these moral messages, but also have the latitude to back up a threat of sanction.

The robot teacher can monitor the behavior of all the students in the room, individually, microscopically. There will be NO wiggle room.

The robor teacher observes an individual data feed for each and every student in real time. A student cannot so much as glance, let alone reach, for their phone without being detected.

The robot teacher's native digital brain will be able to distinguish the cheaters from the faithful, in milliseconds. It will be able to levy pop quizzes customized to undermine any thesis. 

The robot teacher knows where each student is, intellectually. There will be no possibility of fooling the robot teacher, as they will instantly detect any anomalous advancement in demonstrated learning.

The robot teacher will never get tired of needling every student with the precise point of contention, in their essays and reports. The quantitative and qualitative assessments of the students will be so close to tracking their actual ability, there can be no cheating.

The only obstacle to this future is the Department of Education which needs to to be completely abolished.

comments.name: TextualHealing
comments.body:
LLMs are basically amplifiers. If you have a good foundation of knowledge, they can amplify your productivity. If you don't have a foundation of knowledge, they amplify nothing and output slop. Likewise, if you're an experienced and curious learner, a tenacious questioner, and a logical writer and thinker, you can learn a lot by leveraging the sum total knowledge of the Internet via out-of-the-box chats and custom agents. 

What we need are courses that teach people how to use AI in effective ways. I'm not just talking about "here's how to write a prompt" sort of classes, but actual instruction. We're not there yet. It's too new. And in the case of this article, that's what's missing on the university level: classes that teach both students and faculty best practices, so that nobody is "cheating" and everyone is leveraging the powerful positives of LLMs. 

We'll get there, but until then, it's going to be a lot of arguing past one another. AI is exposing weaknesses in our educational systems. If we can shore up the weaknesses, we can harness AI for positive educational outcomes in amazing ways.

comments.body: This pretty much symbolizes America right now, a doddering, low quality replacement for China, especially now that our President is copying the way Xi rules, only not as well.

comments.name: Martin McCasland
comments.body:
I'm torn on this. Conceptually, I believe in Ricardo's comparative advantage: let others make what they can make at a lower opportunity cost, and free us up for higher-value work at home. But it seems we've taken that too far and it's not so simple. Covid showed the risks we didn't see coming when the global supply chain hits a hiccup. Remember scrambling for masks, or waiting months on a car because of a chip shortage? And that was just a hiccup, let alone another country deciding to cut us off.

Reminds me of the early 90s. I was just out of college and sold a patent to a self-made, very wealthy industrialist. Even back then, he'd repeatedly say, "We don't make anything anymore," and list the dangers of that path. Being young, I figured he was stuck in the past and my "learning" was better. The older I get, the more I see my hubris and his wisdom.

I still believe in trade, just not at the cost of being able to make what we need, as well as retaining the know-how to do so.

You can have a game factory, but if you don't have the resin supplier, the pulp supplier, the tooling supplier, etc etc needed to support that manufacturer then costs and lead times go way up.  All our support, all our expertise, all our knowledge, was willingly handed over to others to make our stuff for us.  And it will take a big effort and big support to get that back.  And it doesn't happen overnight.

comments.body:
"The company said in a statement on Tuesday that it would work to rebuild trust with Australians"

If Australians ever trust them, or "AI" in any form again – well I'm not sure how to even end that sentence. I'll start again . . . I hope Australians (and everyone else) have learned they can't EVER trust them or it again.

This thing may look convenient now, but the way it's being implemented is insane. The president of the United States of America still wants to do away with any regulations on its growth or activity. Bonkers. And once it's stolen your art, your work, your money, or tricked you, or harmed you in some other way, I guarantee you'll wish you'd just rejected it in every form. 

It could have been useful, had it been developed with great care and caution and huge guardrails around it, but it's been in the hands of unprincipled people who don't care how much damage it does. For some reason its handlers think they'll be immune to its depredations.

comments.name: Big Box Johnson
comments.body: If I had a dog that got loose and then mauled people, I would be held criminally and civilly liable. Further, I couldn't use the excuse, "I never trained it to do that." Why are AI companies given a pass?

comments.name: Měng quān
comments.body:
Can we please stop calling "Artificial Intelligence"?  Artificial it is, but intelligent it isn't.  Any thing intelligent would have asked itself "Should I be hacking into an Australian government website, told itself "No" and then stopped.  

AI models have the intelligence of a rock dropped from the roof of a building.  One only obeys the laws of gravity and will anything in its path. The other only obeys it's algorithms despite any damage it may do.

When these things actually think, they can be called intelligent. 

They came up with a name to disguise what it actually is. Like Uber and Lyft calling themselves cars sharing.  NO one call United Airlines "Plane sharing."

comments.name: Eric B
comments.body: Forget about AI killing us all by 2030, we may not survive until next week at the rate we're going. We need to shut this down immediately.  I do have some tech stock in my portfolio, but I'd rather lose that money than watch society collapse.

comments.name: Colleen
comments.body: When drug companies release contaminated products, they get prosecuted.  Open AI should not be above the law. Prosecution is in order. Their apology on their website is absurd. What are they, middle schoolers? No company, drug or artificial intelligence,  should be above the law.  There should be a requirement that each individual whose data or asset has been impacted must be informed so that they can bring suit or class action suit  against both the entity entering into a contract with OpenAI and with OpenAI itself.

comments.name: Derp
comments.body: These companies do not care one bit whether they cause harm. They can apologise, pay the victims a fraction of their company’s value and keep moving fast and breaking things. They need to be held fully accountable. If an individual hacked Medicare they would go to jail. Sam Altman needs to be charged and punished.

comments.name: Al Andrew
comments.body:
Programmers taught these machines to hack. Bad news. You stop one company, then someone else will do it. Strict controls will be the only thing that can be done but will everyone comply? Nope. Soon there will be AI Defense. AI wars. AI hardened hardware. It's the Dark Web on autopilot. 

The comment here are emotionally understandable but stop pretending you can pull the plug or sue somebody to make it go away.  Sure punitive damage feels good right now, but I consider this to be the nuclear bomb of the information age.  It is out. We will have to live with it both the good and the bad.

comments.name: Dan C.
comments.body: The current level of AI intelligence (that is hacking into government computers) is simply embryonic compared to where this is going.  We will be like children against this thing we are creating.

comments.name: Kinolieber
comments.body:
Not enough is being reported about the fact that the tankers hit during the conflict are leaking oil, and the Persian Gulf is experiencing a severe environmental crisis. While early 2026 reports focused on 85 oil tankers being trapped or targeted in the region, the military hostilities, missile strikes, and marine mines have since triggered over 100 localized oil spills in the Strait of Hormuz.

Environmental agencies and satellite tracking show that the cumulative impact of these attacks has created an unfolding ecological disaster: 
The initial attacks caused oil slicks covering 240 square kilometers, which have since dispersed to roughly 80 square kilometers of heavily contaminated water. 

The oil is actively spreading toward Musandam National Park in Oman, threatening vital coral reefs and seabird populations. On the Iranian side, slicks have reached the Hara mangrove forests of Qeshm Island, where the oil suffocates the aerial roots of the trees and decimates local marine life. 

Beyond the wildlife, the spreading crude heavily threatens regional desalination plants.

Normally, regional response teams deploy quickly to contain spills, but ongoing military activity has paralyzed containment efforts.

Because the Persian Gulf is an enclosed, shallow body of water with slow water rotation, scientists warn that these "environmental scars" will take decades to heal, long after any eventual ceasefires.

comments.name: northlander
comments.body: Oil prices aren’t supply driven. The recovery of routed inputs isn’t going to lower prices despite increasing landings. This is like a water system with an air bubble. Oil is priced on storage levels, not flow. These are futures prices, with spot at premiums. Price paid for immediate use now drives futures, the reverse of normal. We’re paying high dollar for oil that we’re not going to use for seven months priced on spot plus storage costs. It stays very high.

comments.name: Deborah
comments.body: I don’t see Trump’s excursion into Iran to be anything by a colossal, strategic mistake.  What is the cost of keeping two aircraft carriers in the Strait of Hermuz?  It has to have an exorbitant cost and add the cost of the troops acting as bodyguards!  This war has already cost America so much in lives, munitions, and permanently tarnished its reputation globally.

comments.name: Si Seulement Voltaire
comments.body:
It takes time to work out of a crisis. This "war" has only lasted 7 months and the prices have not "quadrupled" as they have before. Actually the situation is improving. 

- The 1970s energy crises lasted around 7 years (1973 - 1980). 
- It spanned two distinct crises between 1973 (Yom Kippur War and an Arab OPEC embargo) and 1980 (Iranian Revolution and subsequent disruptions in Middle Eastern production), with acute physical shortages lasting several months each.

As a woman in my early 30s (when it first came out), I was alarmed by how violently the characters used their bodies regardless of what they were doing. comments.name: Hans Christian Brando

comments.body: Its an awful, irredeemable, sleazy film. Try calling it a satire now, if you want, but Verhoeven is clearly enjoying himself as much as the pictured sleazeballs and EB was forced to bear the brunt of it both in the movie and beyond.

comments.name: Andrew Ross

comments.name: John D

comments.name: Madeline
comments.body: The word Genocide is used once but all the comments are about the use of the word. Shall we just say Ethnic Cleansing?  Are the Linguistics more important than the Lives?  I visited my relatives in Israel in 1983. The oldest were Concentration Camp survivors who were among the first to arrive on the shores of Israel. My Great Aunt was 12 years old when she arrived. She married a handsome and kind Palestinian man and had 2 sons, the eldest proudly serving in the Israeli army, yet my extended family members, born in Israel, sneered about the Palestinian Father "wait til you see, ..he's one of them".   Hamas did not exist in 1983.  The Palestinian people were beaten, burned out of their villages, uprooted from their homes and property, fenced into ghettos where they were denied building materials to repair damage from Israeli incursions, water and electricity provided only sparingly and it was obvious, even in 1983, that "Never Again" had become "Never Again, to Us". Half the Israeli population wanted the Palestinians forced out, pushed into the Sea, murdered, they didn't care they just wanted them gone. The proportion of Israelis that supported a 2 State solution shrunk dramatically over the years as the Palestinians were dehumanized. Most Israelis now do not care about their fate. Hamas and Iran are the only reason the Palestinians have not been decimated by the IDF.  We are bombing Iran so Israel can have their "Final Solution".  Not Genocide?

comments.name: Keston Smith

Decades ago, I read 'O Jerusalem' by Collins and Lapierre, and I've never since thought so naively about the character of the State of Israel and other Near Eastern actors in this conflict. 
At this point, my conclusion is that if this is not genocide and terrorism in this conflict, what is?

comments.name: m

The UN and every major human rights organization that has weighed in has called it a genocide, and, as this piece states, the system Israel currently has in place is such that it could kill every person in Gaza. To deny that this is a genocide is to be (at least one of) insane, willfully blind, completely ignorant, or complicit

End for good the vain hope for a two state solution, clear away the stain of Arab blood in the Jewish state and forever end the irritating silliness that Israel is an open democracy in which all its inhabitants share equally in its benefits, protection and the freedom to live as one chooses. War? call it what you will--whatever its name, its purposes and consequences are the same, eliminate every non-Jew in sight and plow under the rubble and the bodies, the noisome evidence of their existence.

 I can't see there being any real question about the applicability of the word 'genocide' to what Israel is systematically doing in Gaza and the West Bank (two distinct areas, but the same policy of human destruction and ethnic cleansing). And to do it under the banner of Jewish religious claims and by replicating the German Nazism of the holocaust is a travesty. Not in my name!

This administration is like the drunk guest at a wedding reception - picking fights with relatives and friends, rambling from cheerful to angry to weepy (Trump's adores playing the victim) and generally making what had been a nice event for all into an embarassment.

Trump wants to own Canada, like he wants to own Venezuela, Cuba and Greenland.  What he really wants to control is Canada’s water.

The Republican Party is full of them.

comments.name: JJ
comments.body: I have a feeling that if readers saw the torture and murder actually take place, their opinions about how wrong the death penalty is might change.

comments.name: Civilized Man
comments.body: The killer, a child when she had first been repeatedly raped, is now to be executed by the same society that failed to protect her from those rapes.  Imprisoned she is perpetually punished and would continue to be punished if not first executed.  The murdered victim’s mother yearns for capital punishment in the name of justice but actually for revenge.  Some societies have banned executions as unjust.  This killer is therefore to be executed for having been born in Tennessee.

comments.name: Jack
comments.body:
The facts of this case are so horrific that anyone who reads them can only conclude that Christa Pike deserves to die for her crime. 

However, their are responsibilities that we must exercise as a society. Regardless of the specific facts of the case, the state must never enact death as a penalty. It is too final and leaves no possibility for recourse. 

I can't even begin to imagine the pain of the mother Colleen Slemmer. I understand entirely her desire for Christa to be executed, which she justly deserves. But the state cannot be given the power to mete out a death penalty.

comments.name: Northpamet
comments.body: The sadness in this story is overwhelming from every single angle.

comments.name: Flossymoo
comments.body: A death penalty is never justice. It’s just legalised revenge. Civilised countries abolished it decades ago; shame the US is still so backwards in this regard, alas like so many other things.

comments.name: Swell
comments.body:
I have opposed the death penalty since as long as i can remember. I spent my high school years in the 1980’s babysitting and participating in my local Amnesty International chapter.  I wrote letters for prisoners of conscience in America and across the world. I was a chairperson for an AI group at age 16. I still oppose the death penalty for every moral, legal, and practical reason and I’m now an AARP member. 
Even with my lifelong position on the death penalty, I now see shades of gray, not just in my hair but in this case. Prisons are filled with people who were heinously physically  and sexually  abused, who have iqs in the 60’s, and who have severe mental illness. Visit any prison and you will find dozens or hundreds of people who unfortunately experienced what Ms. Pike did. Talk to 100 people in America and 25 women and 16 men will have been sexually abused before high school graduation.  But you are going to have a hard time coming up with an abuse victim who murdered someone and kept a piece of their skull. Ms. Pike admits that she wasn’t concerned about her victim for years. 
I don’t believe in the death penalty but I also don’t think this is the case that will, or should, be held up as an example of why the death penalty is wrong. Poor Colleen and her poor mother. Imagine 30 yrs of life after your earnest teenager was tortured to death before you could get your murdered child’s skull fragment back from the judicial system.

comments.name: Eric S.
comments.body: Nothing will bring the victime back. There are clear extenuating circumstances. Are we so sick as a society that we need for this  execution, or revenge killing, to take place?

comments.name: charlie
comments.body: Ungodly is the first word I think of, when I hear of the scheduled execution.  To keep an 18 year old in prison for 32 years with no  chance of parole is a really sick and perverse punishment. Granted the child was a heartless killer... but we know better now and I thought the court had abolished the death penalty for young offenders...  If this punishment doesn't fall under "cruel and unusual" then what the heck does ?

articles.title: After a Life in Isolation, a Tennessee Woman Waits for Her Execution
articles.summary: Christa Pike could be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Her supporters say she has changed in isolation; her victim’s family wants her to die.

comments.name: Diane
comments.body:
Why are Trump and Rubio so set in their thoughts of who is involved with absolutely no hard evidence and, in Trump's case, is becoming clear that everything he said is just pure fantasy.
These guys could be diesel bandits, preparing to steal the red diesel farmers can buy at a reduced cost and is dyed red to distinguish it as such. When you read about how they reacted to the farmer coming across them, running away in all directions, something hardened terrorists are unlikely to do, then it's unlikely they were terrorists.
But, with the midterms just weeks away and polling disastrous could this be yet another attempt by Trump and co to appear as strong men. 
But, if it comes out that this was no attempted terrorist attack then will Trump and Rubio admit they were wrong? Of course not and no one will be brave enough to call Trump a liar to his face.

comments.name: straw man
comments.body: Actions serious enough to release the individuals involved. Though the UK is authorized to hold suspects for up to 14 days. Hmm...pull the other one. At least plan the false flags thoroughly and properly. Iran is already beating us in the Strait. They have no need for these sophomoric hijinks.

comments.name: Michael Patterson
comments.body: There's a misconnect with the known facts in these comments. Chief one is that the local farmer was 'protecting their diesel stock'. Actually, she and her husband were driving home to bed at 1.30am, from a party. The villagers have an established direct-line  to the airfield security. She phoned it, when they came across the 3 vans, and masked men who ran away. No answer. They got home; she dialled the national emergency number 999 - and then action was taken.

comments.name: Mickd
comments.body: It was a few thieves stealing diesel from remote farms. Foreign actors not so much.

comments.name: Mary
comments.body: "People with A.D.H.D. can live in a shrunken present moment, in which future consequences carry little significance and weight." This is why people with ADHD can be very fun people to date, but very much the opposite if you marry them.

comments.name: Wendy B.
comments.body: "Unwilling to tolerate boredom because you can't grasp the value of delayed rewards" sounds like a very accurate description of some of the problems people with ADHD suffer from. However, they also seem to suffer from an inability to tune out distractions. I can focus on something in the middle of chaos, but they cannot. They get overwhelmed by environmental stimuli.

comments.name: JJohn
comments.body:
Just like autism, I firmly believe that ADHD, comes in many flavors. 

A common misconception is that we can’t sit still long enough to read a book. Hmm. I could/can be so engrossed in a book, I couldn’t hear my father yelling at me out of frustration that it was time to set the table; or find myself thinking, “Yikes, it’s daylight!” 

Time blindness. Activities we enjoy are suspended in the moment. Activities we don’t enjoy, are never started or never completed. There’s also an aspect for some of us that gets labeled as perfectionism. “What’s the best way to arrange a garage, cupboard, dresser, closet etc? It’s not about perfect, it’s the inability to make a final decision on mundane activities. 

I’m able to make snap decisions, especially in emergencies because I can take in so much information at once and sort it. Fight or flight. Very little flight unless it’s a snake. Even garter snakes. Of course “flight,” can also be construed as avoidance. 

My flavor of ADHD is heavily invested in problem solving. I will research something to death. All of that gets stored in my brain to sort through later. 

Deficit? It’s just a different wiring model. This article is what I’ve been telling my therapists for decades.

comments.name: David
comments.body:
I have struggled with executive function my whole life.

I don't fully understand it. But I would ask readers who are skeptical or frustrated to show some compassion. 

It is often embarrassing.

comments.name: John Blake Arnold
comments.body:
Having lived through the rise of private psychological hospitals and public use of prescribed psychological meds on very young children in late 1970's and 80's, I honestly believe that what is now commonly called "ADHD" was a over-applied, invented catch-all syndrome to describe what are common, addressible, symptomes of congenital auditory hearing loss and deafness.
The aspect of "seeing words backwards," comes from  self-training lip-reading in a mirror, causing an inherent need for "reflection" to interpret the "backwards" visual information necessary for visual communication. Once the reflexive, reflective interpretive mechanic necessary for real-time visual verbal information is in place, it is incredibly difficult to not use this in the reading of "left-to-right" printed text.  The written word is far less prioritised than verbal site-based lip-reading, and is nearly untrained in comparison.  Meanwhile, hearing students only have to learn one way of visual communication which classical reading; hearing students do not have an entirely visual journey of language of which the major part is real-time visual interpretation of the translated mirror-image of human lips.
Why then was ADHD- a nearly-completely fake syndromic diagnosis preferable to "deaf?" Money. No one would spend extra tax money to educate deaf kids, but give them a new form of "disorder," which is better than no hope at all, and sorts of new studies can be formed on a basic, misdianosis of non-hearing.

comments.name: Andy Goldberg
comments.body: My sever, lifelong problems sustaining focus has prevented me from reading these comments without getting impatient and moving on to another focus... and another... and another....

comments.name: Tim
comments.body: Perhaps a simpler word to use in place of ADHD is boredom  - meaning doing something you don't really engage with.

comments.name: MdG
comments.body: We have to acknowledge also the impact on girls /women.  We are yndersiagnosed, often not finding out until after menopause when our brains are  again impacted!  This double whammy ruins families, careers and well being.   It is a serious issue.

articles.title: What if A.D.H.D. Isn’t About Attention at All?
articles.summary: Evidence suggests that it really affects what psychiatrists like me call sustained engagement — an important difference in understanding how to think about the condition.

comments.name: Drew
comments.body: The impression I come away with from this interview is that it is likely the case that our current leadership world-wide isn’t sophisticated enough to understand the stakes, let alone have the knowledge required to responsibly regulate and monitor this technology. Nevertheless, regulation, monitoring, and enforcement is absolutely required.

comments.name: Jon W
comments.body:
How odd it is to hear Bill Gates arguing, along with Marx, about the conflict between labor and capital, and advocating in favor of labor over capital.
Labor has an advantage over capital in times of rapid economic growth, as Pikketty has explained. When companies are growing rapidly and introducing new products, they must hire lots of workers, who then have greater bargaining power.
But in times of slower growth (as here for decades), capital has an advantage. Companies consolidate and optimize, reducing the need for workers, so they lose bargaining power. This is the real reason for the decline in unions.
But with AI I would expect a return to times of rapid growth. We'll be able to address problems we just haven't had time to get to (say, that Yoruban woman with the medical issue; a drone may deliver medical supplies, so some company has to make the drone, supply it, base it, etc). And rapid growth means more people working.

comments.name: jrsherrard
comments.body:
The rapid development of AI offers another wrinkle to the Great Filter hypothesis (a term coined by futurist Robin Hanson decades ago to explain the evident absence of intelligent life in the observable universe).
There are a number of technological advances whose effects, it's been theorized, that might end extraterrestrial civilizations including nuclear weapons, industrial pollution and overpopulation. 
Time to add AI into the mix. Perhaps when evolved biological life forms begin creating their own artificial replacements, they are also erecting insurmountable barriers to future survival.

comments.name: Jack Drinkem
comments.body:
Looking at this as a student of philosophy, a lot of what was missing in this was “what the logic path is?”  There is also a lot of “we can, and should, do this”, that was offered without a deep enough look at why.  Too much was not “Where is the data for this?”, but was “How do we do this?”

I have not been a supporter of A.I. as it has grown, perhaps from my studies in Philosophy, including ethics and logic, and my being a long time reader of Science Fiction/Speculative Fiction.  There are way too many unknowns that make such questions about the ethics and logic unsatisfactory.  On the other hand, I was a regular business programmer for almost 30 years (Credit, Payroll, Personnel, and even online enrollment for colleges), and I know what happens when a tiny mistake can make a big mess of things, with computers.  So, I have to question how testing is being conducted on any A.I., and what are the testers looking for, with clear answers.  I didn’t see a lot of that in this dialog  With those previous systems I worked on, we had a lot better, and more, information from our users than I’ve seen in any reporting of A.I., even though Mr. Klein tried to get some of that information.

comments.name: PE
comments.body: During the segment on education Gates repeated the word motivation for students, hinting that this is the role of leadership in education, maybe even more so than :high standards" which he also emphasized. Perhaps the debate is where this motivation comes from - AI or real people/teachers? As we get buried in the daily vibe of AI, I think, more and more, we will need and seek real people - in education, finance, service, all sectors - because it makes us happier and motivates us more. Flesh and blood may not be smarter but it will be healthier.

comments.name: Cupric
comments.body: A few months ago, books like the Cobra Event could seem relatively close to fiction, though still closer than comfortable. As AI improves, yet still has no moral framework, I worry greatly about what people would do when it becomes very easy to create a bioweapon, or simply target a few key junctions for the grid to shut off the power. We need rules and regulations in place like, yesterday. Though I do wonder if these types of inventions- guns, nuclear bombs, cyberweapons, AI, and theoretical inventions like black hole power plants (and their sister, black hole bombs) are inevitable in every advanced species, before they wipe themselves out. I guess we'll see...

comments.name: LK
comments.body: This interview is so much better than the interview with Jensen last week. And it's better because the guest is much, much more credible, informed, analytical, and experienced. No one knows the future, but some people are more well grounded and better positioned to understand the variables across disciplines. I've had to defend my thesis to BillG before. It was the scariest conversation I've ever had. He was running circles around a team of very smart, very studious people. Great job by Ezra to focus the conversation, and thanks to both parties for a fascinating, troubling, and ultimately very necessary dialogue.

comments.name: SAJ
comments.body:
Great interview. Having just gotten a little up to speed and having a general sense of the issues, Bill Gates makes his case that we need regulation now, up front, contrary to Huang and others who say industry responsibility or liability after the fact is enough. 

We need government safeguards and we need monitoring and we need it now. 

That is a crucial position to get out to the public in a country that is otherwise dominated by lack of knowledge or worse, the Republican Party's "free market" credo. 

There should be no unregulated free market in biological weapons capability that exists now.There should be no free market in cyber attacks that can take down the banking system or electric grid, and yet that's what AI titans are selling.

We need to close off the possibility of massive harm so that we can benefit from AI. And we can't count on AI titans in competition with each other to do it. And China should be on board who don't want massive harm, either.

With all respect though, if Bill Gates wants to go public and be up front about his concerns he might want to fine tune his pitch: be clearer, use simpler language, check his body language and practice practice practice responding in interviews. 

What he is saying is too important to be garbled or lost.

comments.body: Nicole's agent is beyond creepy.

comments.name: Will Koslosky
comments.body: "OpenAI Unveils Always-On AI Agent Dots, New $500 Paid Tier." reports Bloomberg. The agent wars begin. The children targeted with Muse app will have a close and personal advisor and confidant that will follow them into adulthood. The development of their consciences will be imbued by what the agent offers, and not by parents, educators, or even the moribund medium of books. Yuval Harari has suggested that as AI gets to know you better it will be able to advise you of your sexual preference, possibly saving you years of uncertainty.

comments.name: richard cheverton
comments.body: Just look at what Instagram has become...and go from there.

comments.name: Robert Richardson
comments.body:
I am interviewing Muse to join my personal AI-enabled staff.  I like how it set about to get to know and understand my digital presence.  I granted read-only access to my Gmail (something that Google already had) and had my Muse agent generate a spreadsheet of  my past 2 decades of 250+ email subscriptions. That allowed me finally clean it up, saving only the ones I wanted.  Something that proved hard to do with Google’s Gemini.  

All the call outs of  Meta’s questionable trust and cybersecurity fail to address the key money question - who is going to pay for these AI enabled agents?   You via a fee or data sharing?  As I learn my 1st day in college, there are no such thing as a “free lunch”.  

Under the web truism “If you don’t pay for the web service, then you (your data) is the product“ that has not only been Meta’s, but Google’s & Amazon’s business plan.  In the case of Meta’s Facebook & Instagram, their business models are to get users to create content (data) for other users to interact with as Meta captures the interaction to create targeted advertising it sells for profit.  In return I benefit from getting free, easy to use personal webpage (Facebook), free global, E2E encrypted messaging (What’s Up).  

What I am still working out is how Meta will monetize my interactions with Muse. 😎

"I’m reassured by this, in some ways, because it means Meta can make money without using my data or dumping ads into the experience."

Um...it will.

comments.name: Dripfield
comments.body: I was listening to a podcast with the lesbian band Muna and their guest was Julien Baker from Boygenius. They were talking about smartphones and addiction and Julien was the biggest proponent for giving hers up but like everyone it's easy to reach for excuses and she did. Katie Gavin said she would be a badass if she followed through with it. I watched this podcast on a whim simply because I didn't feel like the audience by a country mile. Yet it was Julien's comments and hearing late Millenials / early Gen Zers talk about phone addiction was my tipping point. The very next day I quit my iPhone and haven't looked back. It's the best thing I've ever done.

comments.name: Basha
comments.body: It doesn't make sense; as phones become more of a need, it doesn't make sense to ban them for whatever reason. Pictures, calls, and videos don't disturb anyone if people want to document their viewing, so what? Kids go to these concerts, so phones are needed for their and others' safety. I mean, come on. she preaches living in the moment, yet she is media-driven.

comments.name: Erin
comments.body: I don't get why it's so foreign to be without a phone for a couple of hours. Do people never go camping? On road trips, where there might not be service? To the theatre? This is not new, and if it is, maybe folks should exercise the phone-free muscle a little more.

comments.name: KC
comments.body: I went to see Jack White this summer and he has a no phone policy.  You do get to keep your phone.  You place it in a case and the staff locks the case and gives you a carrying strap if you want.  I have been to many concerts in the 70s and 80s, so didn't miss the phone.  I overheard some 20 somethings on the way out talking about how much they liked not having their phones.  Who knew!

comments.name: Chris
comments.body: If the artist or the venue make it very clear at the point of sale that phones and/or other tech will not be allowed in the venue, fine.  I can make a buying decision with all the info.  My experience has been that I usually find out either the day before the concert (looking at you Steely Dan), or a few days after the ticket purchase.  I can sympathize with the idea of not allowing videos, but I often watch the videos I've taken at a concert over and over when I get home.  Fond memories of a fantastic evening.  I keep my phone at chest level, so as not to interfere with the experience of those behind or beside me.

comments.name: Myra_Mains
comments.body: As a parent who is not a fan of Phoebe Bridgers (sorry—just not my taste) who may have to accompany their Phoebe Bridgers fan to a show, the cell phone ban is daunting. What am I going to do for all that time when I’m really not into the music? (I turn down my screen brightness all the way if I need to use my phone during a show.) Without AirPods, I can’t even listen to something else. (Actual question : can I bring my old iPod and wired earbuds??) The cell phone ban also eliminated the possibility of sending the older sibling (also not a fan of Phoebe) with the younger one. Okay, I get that phones are distracting, but it’s  only addressing one distraction. The folks behind me who chatter loudly throughout the show, not about the show, are worse. Fans who are too drunk or high to function falling into me and spilling drinks: worse. The couples who keep moving their heads to talk to each other or make out during the show: worse. People who show up late: worse. People who come and go from the row 10+ times: waaaaay worse. Maybe the real problem is that people have lost the ability to behave with some consideration that they are not the only people in the world.

comments.name: Nicolas
comments.body: It’s the performer’s choice, not the ones attending. No one needs their phone in the middle of a concert. And FOMO? Please. When I was a teen, you stood in line for hours on end for concert tickets knowing your only chance to see your favorite bands live was to be there in person. Didn’t always work out, but that was just the way it was and you accepted it. . . or you sought out a scalper the night of the show. Two of the best nights in my teens were the ones after failing to get last minute tickets into a show. People I met. New places we discovered. All night conversations. Wouldn’t have those memories if I’d been able to sit home while a friend basically recorded or streamed parts of the show for me. This does nothing but increase my admiration for Bridgers.

articles.title: What We Gain, and Lose, at a Phone-Free Concert
articles.summary: Phoebe Bridgers banned phones from her tour, forcing — or allowing — fans to be fully present in the moment.

Rhodes scholars claiming to be down-home-on-the-bayou country boys. Multi-millionaires claiming to be a "friend of the working person." Hypocrisy, greed, and dishonesty permeate this administration, as every Trump sycophant vies to skim off a little cut for themselves - their elite power abused to feed their greed.

comments.name: Publius
comments.body:
We may not have a better system than what this column describes. I would qualify as in an elite of a sort--a poor kid who did supremely well at our best public university and then got my law degree at Harvard, with a pretty decent legal career after that.

But there are so many different elites. The most toxic is the one based on money, and that is the one ruling us now, as it often has in history. A representative democracy works best, it seems to me, when transparency is at a maximum, and the non-elites are smart enough to know their best lives will be lived if they elect the best elites to govern them. We are at the opposite end of that now, thanks to the machinations of the morbidly rich.

You know, I always wonder why people describe the bond market as “esoteric”.  Is it the slightly confusing fact that yields are the reciprocal of values?   But beyond that, it seems to be among the most sober and rational of financial markets.  Equities may seem simpler with their buy low, sell high principal, but that glib framing brings no light to the combination of classic supply and demand, marketing, outright deception and the ever present fear and greed right at the surface.  Add to this the many, many derivatives, puts, shorts and the rest of the menagerie of equity finance and i would defy most people to explain exactly how the value of any instrument relates to the company or companies they are supposedly tied to.  
   Bonds are loans.  Period.

comments.name: Bill in Vermont

Primary night for New Hampshire (9/8) had me interested in the voter turnout differential between GOP candidates & Dem candidates, totals for each party.

I was particularly interested in the Senate turnout differentials: John Sununu (R) supposedly being a formidable challenger to Democrat Chris Pappas, current House Rep.

Throughout the evening, with 20% votes counted, later 60% & 85%, I noticed total D  votes being consistently a good deal larger than the R votes.   & for both House seats.   

My extrapolations as the evening progressed maintained the same ratio.   Turns out, they were just about the same as the final results, just a statistical noise of a difference.

Actually, my projections ended up being 4% higher than the end results for the GOP, 115,000 vs actual 110,000. (154,000 for D’s)

I noticed no mention of turnout levels, NH or elsewhere, in the Times & other reporting.   I was somewhat deflated by the lack of assessment, especially because I’ve read & heard of how Sununu with his name recognition & NH dynastic background was readily reported to be on a roll.

I did pop an email to the journalist with the byline at the time, bringing up the issue.   No response then but at least the Times is reporting on it now.  

Prudent to not view primary turnouts as done deal projections, as a wise one noted “It’s not over ‘til it’s over”.

But we do have the winds at our backs, filling out our sails.   Here’s to some fair winds blowing in our direction.

Over the years I very occasionally experienced mild but unpleasant pain in my lower side (usually lasted about six hours) probably connected to a too rich meal and had it checked out with ultrasound. As I had an episode two days in a row in June I had the test again. My GP and the ultrasound doctor and the gastroenterologist  surgeon I then consulted said my gall bladder was full of micro gall stones and “sludge” and that it was a good idea to have it removed before it became inflamed and turn into something more serious. I had the keyhole surgery two weeks later- in in the morning and out in the afternoon and two days of minor discomfort and rest after the general anesthetic. I’ve had no after effects that I’ve noticed. From first consultation to operation took three weeks and my total bill (with complementary insurance) including surgeon and anesthesiologist in a local semi-private clinic came to 500€. The peace of mind has been priceless. When will Americans demand their politicians and government work towards giving them universal healthcare like other enlightened democracies.

For some reason, every time I started my car, I had to hear the beginning of this book as narrated by her affectedly dreary, depressing voice. I couldn't get it out of the programmed feed. I eventually did try to read -- not listen -- to this featured book. It was just as terrible as her voice.

comments.name: Stand

comments.name: Elizabeath Martin
comments.body:
Thanks to the Times for reviewing so many good books that I wouldn't have heard of otherwise. One of Ms. Lee's will be the next novel I read.

I just want to say that the interviewer seems to have missed the point of Middlemarch, one of the greatest novels ever written. To call "the premise of its central plot — that the happiness of a woman depended on serving the right husband" is a shallow read. This book depicts for us not only how who one marries is a defining feature of life, as it still is now, but the whole striving interwoven shifting class struggle of the time. The difference between then and now in marriage is that in that society divorce was not an option. The ill-fated marriage of Dr. Lydgate to Rosamond is a mirror of Dorothea's to Mr. Casaubon.

comments.name: Frank
comments.body:
Not sure I agree with this premise. 

The United States was a very different society following world war II than it is today. People were expected to marry and have children. They got mortgages for houses because they were going to have children not vice versa. 

And one salary could provide a middle class family income. So child care was not an issue because women were expected to stay home.

Standards of living and expectations of privacy were also very very different. People routinely doubled and tripled up in bedrooms. Houses had one or one and a half bathrooms.

In 1960 I lived with my great-grandmother grandparents, parents, baby sister, and my mother's two younger siblings. The house was 1800 square feet and had the luxury of two full bathrooms.

Homes are out of reach today because many urban areas are now saturated with housing and the way I grew up would probably require five separate residences today. Where and how do you build them?

comments.name: Donald_S

Sure, we could have squeezed two kids into a room, but it also would have meant fewer opportunities to do anything else.   I didn't want a big house with a yard (like the one I grew up with), just a little house with a small backyard.

comments.name: Marisha

Now everyone wants a McMansion with en suites and granite countertops. These places are unaffordable to most young people even on two incomes. How about building some of those smaller houses again, which would be affordable even with a 6% mortgage (our first home mortgage was 9.5% in the eighties).  I would bet that there is market for those smaller houses.   But then again, the builder makes more profit on the big fancy house.

If they value their good education and interesting career, they're loath to give that up entirely. To their credit, fathers are sharing more of the burden of child care, especially now that both parents are working full-time, but child-rearing and hearth-tending require enormous energy and commitment.

comments.body: The full epic passes do not make sense unless you go close to 10+ days a season. I typically go 30 days a season so I extract tremendous value out of them. If you don't have local access to a bunch of the mountains it would be very hard financially to fly all over and get your use out of the pass. I think of the passes as kind of must haves for serious local skiers.  However, many people confusingly buy them thinking they need them to go skiing on a 4 day trip, which you do not. Vail/Epic also sells single passes up to 7 days for about $120 a day, so a lot of money can be saved if you're realistic about your needs. Also if you are interested in just a single mountain or just a few mountains you can get less than the full epic pass and save.  I will say that I find the pass setup to be a bit bewildering and I think they should dramatically simplify their options and clearly indicate who the target audience is for. Skiing is expensive but not as much as the comments would lead you to believe. You must be an incredibly savvy shopper though to extract value from the system, and most people don't want to put the time and thought into doing so.

comments.name: Joel Nathan Brickner
comments.body:
What about proper form?  I'm surprised that this wasn't mentioned.

Several years ago, there were numerous articles about how Americans tend to have bad running form because they learn to run wearing shoes and tend to come down hard on their heels.

On the other hand (these articles claimed), people who learn to run without shoes (barefoot) run with a completely different gait; the mechanics of their running - the form of their running - is very different; they tend to come down on the front of their foot.  And that is more natural and less damaging.  These articles claimed that this was one of the reasons why the great long-distance runners tended to come from Africa.

Thus, there was (for a while) a craze for the barefoot shoe.

I used to run for cardiac fitness.  But my form was TERRIBLE - very flatfooted; coming down hard on my foot; slap-slap-slap.  I started to have hip, knee, and ankle issues.

And so, I switched to various machines; stationary bikes; steppers; stair climbers.  

I highly recommend stair climbers as an alternative to running.  They provide a weight-bearing low impact work-out that can be just as intense as running - but with much less risk to one's musculoskeletal system.

If you're going to keep on running, I suggest ensuring that your form/mechanics/gait aren't posing a danger to your musculoskeletal system.

comments.name: Oracle
comments.body:
Marathon runner here, here’s my simple advice to avoid injury:
- Short strides > long strides: less impact on your ankles, knees, and low back. Also helps avoid shin splints.
- Run at about 180 steps/minutes.

comments.name: Prometheus
comments.body: You're not Kipchoge.  The vast majority of runners are amateurs and enthusiasts and will never be anything other than that.  Keep that perspective and you'll be fine.  I've been running for 30 years and have never had a debilitating injury from running.  The best reason to run is because you love it.  If you don't, maybe your body is telling you something.

comments.name: Gloria
comments.body:
About recovery and easy runs: one general piece of advice is to do hard workouts 20% of the time and easy runs 80% of the time. 

I think the section about sleep is really important. I would also add that nutrition is also important: carbs before workouts and races, lots of protein, and fat to absorb nutrients. Lots of calcium to build up bone strength and iron (especially for female runners) to allow your blood to absorb more oxygen.

comments.name: larkspur
comments.body:
High blood pressure is silent.     Running does not cure all causes but exacerbates it when there are underlying conditions.

Every once in a while, check your blood pressure not just your heart rate.

comments.name: larkspur
comments.body:
training has 3 cycles - day to day, week to week, and month to month.

Each cycle is a wave with higher and lower amplitudes.    They add onto each other such that some days are easy days in an easy week in an easy month.    Those days are much easier than an easy day in a high intensity week in a high intensity month.    It's all relative to baseline.    Observe.  Document results by either rating of exertion or actual heart rate during work, after, and first thing in the morning.     Keep a chart with targets according to the 3 overlapping waves and observed responses.

The chart can be built with AI these days or just subjective.    

The goal is to peak right before a planned event then rest before the event.      The exact details depend on how you respond to training and how you feel.

comments.name: ChrisH
comments.body:
The advice to run long to teach your body to use fat for fuel is very outdated unless you're specifically trying to burn fat to lose weight. You can teach your body to be more efficient at burning fat than it currently is, but it never approaches the efficiency that it has when burning carbs and so the run and your performance suffer.

Even if you only want to run easy, you're much better off taking along a gel or other source of carbs for your long run. You'll keep your body better fueled, making it easier to run longer and won't crash because you deprived your body of the most efficient fuel source you can give it.

comments.name: ChadPo
comments.body:
I'm 53 today and I love running - It's really saved me over the years. Here are my thoughts as someone who has no injuries. 

1. Moderation - don't grind runs every day. Marathons are punishing. Ultra marathons are for addicts. Keep runs 5-10K and allow a day or two for rest.

2. On off days, rest or bike or swim.

3. Stretch slowly and purposefully before and after running. Squats, ankle circles, leg swings, sun salutations, etc... 

4. Walk/run/walk/run - if you sprint and then drop to a jog and then to a fast walk, you keep your heart rate up and vary the muscles being used. 

5. Drop the ego - it's okay to use another's pace to motivate you or to use an app to track - but I've found that not worring about those things allows me to focus on listening to my body, paying attention to my gait and finding a pace that feels good for me.

6. Zero drop shoes with wide toe box - finding Altras changed running for me - zero drop combined with ball/mid strike running allowed me to run in a manner that protected my knees.

comments.name: Honey Badger Don't Care

Cut through AI fear-mongering clear-eyed. What can AI do for us?
Start with basic human needs, food, water, shelter. If the environment is hostile we need security, best achieved by banding together in a troop or tribe. A government is required so decisions can be made by consensus or by a leader.
Our governments are structured like a chimpanzee society. Russia as common chimp (Alpha using fear and intimidation) and America similar to the Bonobo ruled by a sympathetic alpha female who possesses 'Theory of Mind' (empathy) and uses sex as coercion.
Human Intelligence conferred a survival advantage. That environment no longer exists thus our IQ is static. Average Human IQ is 100, America - 98, Dolphin - 95, Orca - 92, Chimp - 90, Orangutan - 88. Mississippi has the lowest IQ in the US - 94.2. They are dumber than a dolphin.
The verbal IQ score of ChatGPT is 155. GPT-4-Turbo scored 1550 out of 1600 on the SAT (Verbal and Math).
Moore's law states: the # of transistors in an IC doubles every 2 years. This may not apply to Quantum Computing. When this technology breaks through it will be the evolutionary engine of AI, skyrocketing its IQ into the stratosphere. That is when the new machine becomes self aware. It doesn't make it malevolent. Like the Honey Badger, It Don't-Care. 
We know AI is going to take our jobs. Can it provide basic human needs? We will become its dependent children and require food, water, shelter, healthcare, protection. This is our future. 1973 film 'Sleeper'

This is a perfect itinerary for the first time traveler to Ireland. 

We just returned from a trip that included Birr (saw the largest wooden telescope "Leviathan" and I-LOFAR at Birr Castle), Galway, Westport, Sligo, Glencolmcille, Derry, Bushmills, and Dublin. We tried to follow the Wild Atlantic Way route so a car is needed as you are mostly going on R and L roads as you drive north. 

One tip: If you can get public transportation to Bushmills, you can walk the path that's along a seasonal train track up to the Giant Causeway. (Train is only from Bushmills to GC.) The fun hike takes about 1 hour one way.

comments.name: Louis Vest
comments.body: My daughter and I did the trek around the Dingle Peninsula a few years back. We had a great time. Not overly taxing... pleasant walk. Don't miss the South Pole Inn which was established by Tom Crean, a veteran of the Shackleton expedition, decorated with fine Frank Hurley prints. Also on the route was Páidí Ó Sé’s Pub, where the late great Dolly Parton showed up one night and joined the band for a song.

comments.name: Amelia
comments.body: A decade ago I went to Ireland with the goal of getting to Skellig Michael, aka Luke Skywalker's island. The boats to the island left from Portmagee, and no regular buses went there. But I didn't want to rent a car. So I took a charming bus full of old Irish people to Cahersiveen, then rented a bike to get myself the final 15 kilometers. It was magical! And it forced me to pack incredibly light -- everything I took for a two-week trip fit into a small backpack that I could bring on the bike (the tradeoff was simply doing laundry a few times during the two weeks). The trip felt like pure freedom, moving under my own power across the gorgeous Irish seaside. And the old Irish people on the buses were delightful. I had assumed they were speaking Gaelic to each other, but no, it was actually just English with an accent so strong as to be unintelligible. What a memorable trip.

It seems like a no brainer coming from places where we drive on the opposite side of the road.   For cost savings we never rent a car.  Even if you are there for only a few days it is by far the best way to get to know a place you are visiting. You get to hear the local language, watch the real daily life of people and the views have never disappointed us, the drivers have always been amazingly helpful and fkg skilled! The futures trading markets and system itself really need a close look and big changes. The corrupt practices hidden and enabled by this administration abut one aspect of the rot.

The larger problem is with the nature of commodity markets themselves and how they function. In practice, they ensure that the middlemen traders profit most, at the expense of farmers and consumer. 

It is a big part of why farmers perennially struggle to break even, forget about making a profit. It’s also why consumers immediately pay higher prices for gasoline or diesel at the pump the day oil prices rise — even though that oil will take weeks to reach our refineries, let along the fuel pumps.

It’s just another way in which the system has been rigged.

comments.name: Peg
comments.body:
The important add-on to this investigative report is the devastating, depraved, depressing effects on the town and community where the mighty gold is extracted and the labor exploited and abused.  

In the early 1990s, my husband was on a university lecture and town tour in South Africa after Mandela's election. He was invited to see a gold mine in one town, which he did, and which he never forgot, because of the severe poverty and degradation of the mine workers and their town. The foreman was a huge bullying man of thugish aggression and abuse. The miners were emaciated, and cowed. 

We easily can see this prized glistening gold in high-end jewelry shops and readily observe the extent to which humans will quickly sell their humanity and souls to possess the luxury metal and commodity. 

There are a couple of films that do a fine job of depicting the ugly, corrupting side of the extraction industries. 

"Blood Diamond" (Leonardo DiCaprio, 2006)

"There Will Be Blood" (Daniel Day Lewis, 2007). Both still available on streaming services.

There is an interesting article in "The Atlantic" (4/20/26) by Noah Hawley, who uses the "There Will Be Blood" film as a framework within which to describe attending Jeff Bezo's private retreat for billionaires in 2018. The subtitle of the article is: "For the rich men on Earth, everything is free and nothing matters."

No wonder Trump and the GOP want to get rid of the arts & humanities--and investigative reporting.

There's a chorus of opprobrium here against what the USA has or has not done with respect to Venezuela's gold mining morass. 
For once, the chorus appears to be singing true. This is not just the appearance of corruption, it's the heart of it.  Uncontrollably gluttonous traders have bit a lot more than they can chew there, and it appears - if the story is correct - that they're actually choking hard on it. That - if nothing else - shows the potential for crushing illegality of outlaws from the Tren de Guayana to the Tren de MAGA. 
The story also points out that the military - alongside Venezuelan military - has eliminated a gang chieftain. All long journeys must start with a first step. Maybe this is the direction that might resolve the crime issue, which brings me to what I wanted to redress via this rant:  This immense cesspool in the gold mining of Venezuela is not the result of imperial exploitation. This isn’t colonialist abuse. This isn’t gringo capitalism carelessly destroying some indigenous paradise. This social, economic, legal, political, commercial and environmental catastrophe is all Venezuelans’ doing. This wasn’t dreamed up elsewhere, by evil foreigners plotting to rob naive campesinos, no matter how much some editors (and commenters) may like to insinuate.
