The city doesn’t allow them, supposedly for the same reason this story cites, because stepping on them is disrespectful. How ridiculous. The victims of the Holocaust will forever be crying for any form of memory, and of the human contact they were denied in life. The stones are one of the sweetest, simplest and most human memorials I’ve ever encountered, and if it were me, I would gladly weather endless ignorant footsteps to gain the understanding of just one more person.

comments.name: Gerhard Wittenberg
comments.body:
Years ago, on a visit to Neuruppin, after Germany’s reunification, I made a short video showing the two “Stolperstein” placed just outside our family home, memorializing my aunt (Edith Frank, geboren Anker) and my grandmother (Emma Anker, geboren Wittenberg). 

This short video can be found by searching on Bing for “Gerhard Wittenberg Vimeo.”

At that time, at the local history museum, there was a small dedicated room with documents and objects remembering the events and local families who suffered the consequences of the Holocaust. Last time I went, this exhibit was not there anymore, but I couldn’t find out if the original intent of the exhibit was to have a permanent display or not. 

History is an odd mixture of what do we like to remember and what do we want to erase.

On a different note, the creator of this project, Gunter Demnig, is a great artist.  Painful and disturbing. His work is pertinent, relevant and consequential for our, and future generations.  What do we do with it, it’s a reflection of ourselves. 

Art at its best!

.

Thank you for covering this important issue and for making the connection between this protest and the events at Ridglan Farms. However, as other commenters have already noted, there are several inaccuracies that should be corrected, e.g , the number of marchers is significantly underestimated, as is local support for the march. More importantly, though, the article missed an opportunity to properly frame the debate over animal experimentation.

Thirty years ago, there could have been a real ethical debate about animal testing: Is it okay to torture millions of non-human animals to possibly save or enhance the lives of humans? This is a question that people disagree on.

But given the scientific advances of recent decades, the question today is quite different: Is it okay to torture millions of non-human animals when more than 90% of drugs that pass animal testing fail on humans, and when more effective, human-centered, cruelty-free technologies exist to test drugs and product safety? 

At this point, animal testing is holding science back, and only inertia and entrenched interests are keeping it alive. The FDA no longer requires animal testing, and this cruel process is being phased out. The question now is, how quickly will we modernize? And how many beings will we continue to needlessly torture, and how many effective medical treatments will we fail to develop, while we delay?

comments.name: AC
comments.body: Thank you for covering the historic March to Abolish Animal Testing and the 1,000-strong rally outside the gates of Marshall BioResources, a multinational company that breeds tens of thousands of animals (including beagles, cats, ferrets, and pigs) every year at its facility in upstate New York to be sold for experimentation. According to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the National Institutes of Health, over 95% of new drugs that test safe and effective in tests on animals are shown to be either unsafe or ineffective in humans--a 95% failure rate. This failure (along with the obvious ethical concerns) is at the heart of scientific work to develop human-relevant testing methods. Such methods now exist and are the reason the bipartisan FDA Modernization Act 2.0 (which allows companies to choose non-animal testing methods) was passed overwhelmingly a couple of years ago. Earlier this month, the FDA implemented language in its guidance to companies that clarifies its position that non-animal methods can be used in bringing drugs to market. Animal experimentation apologists have for decades trotted out the claim that we need a full organism to study drugs--but using nonhuman animals to test drugs or other compounds is like using a map of Australia to get from San Francisco to New York. The "animals versus science" is an old, tired trope, and I'm disappointed the NYT insists on clinging to this trope which props up outdated science and ethics.

I’m not noticing semis slowing down at all. Time may be money in the trucking business but speed also has its cost in fuel.
 
Aerodynamic drag determines the fuel necessary to move an object. About 52% of the fuel used by a semi at even low highway speeds is to overcome aerodynamic drag, while for an automobile it’s about a quarter of that.
 
The factors determining aerodynamic drag:
Speed (velocity squared): This is the most powerful factor. Small increases in speed produce large jumps in resistance.
Frontal area: The larger the surface facing the oncoming air, the more resistance you encounter. A semi-truck has far more frontal area than a sports car, which is part of why it needs a much bigger engine to maintain highway speed.
Air density: Thicker air pushes harder. You experience more wind resistance at sea level than at high altitude, and more on a cold day than a hot one, because cold air is denser.
Drag coefficient: This is a single number that captures how “slippery” a shape is. A flat plate perpendicular to airflow has a drag coefficient of about 1.28. A sphere ranges from 0.07 to 0.5 depending on speed and surface texture. A modern sedan typically falls between 0.25 and 0.35. The lower the number, the more easily air flows around the object. The drag coefficient of a semi-truck can vary considerably depending on whether fuel-saving modifications like rounded corners, side skirts and fairings to close the gap between the tractor and trailer are added.

comments.name: John
comments.body:
It is time for a shift of more freight from highways to railroads and as well time for phasing out diesel-guzzling heavy trucks for hybrid diesels.  Long haul diesel trucks get about 8 mpg; a hybrid-electric diesel truck gets about 25% better fuel efficiency.  Meanwhile short haul delivery hybrid vehicles can get 25 mpg; and EV short haul vehicles get effectively 100 mpg.

Why are not the major shippers from UPS to Fedex etc, rapidly replacing their diesel trucks with hybrids and or EV short haul delivery vehicles?   Why is the US Postal Service using local delivery trucks that get 8 mpg and not already at least replaced all of these with gas hybrids if not EVs?

In a perfect world, the federal government would be helping shipper and in addition coordinating a shift of long haul freight from trucks to railcars.   Nobody should be hauling freight from the West to the East Coast in a truck.

The feds should also be helping small truckers as well to purchase the hybrids and EVs.   Cutting burning of diesel will greatly cut air pollution and cut carbon emissions and in our Nation's interest.

comments.body:
“Small trucking companies tend to drive in the right lane when it comes to politics. And they want immediate relief. Simple as that.”
If immediate relief is what they want, Trump can manage that by hook or crook by promising instant cash back from the US Treasury like he has twice done for farmers. But this shortsightedness is what will get these truckers in trouble again. Let us assume truckers again vote for Republicans and they come back in majority. Next day after the mid-term election, each one of these Republicans will change their tune and begin kowtowing to Trump. Now with elections behind, Trump -ever the vengeful one- will resume Iran bombing with all his might and relish to show who is the boss on the world stage. Count on it. And now, Iran retaliates by bombing many Middle East oil countries that are friends with the US. Oil and diesel prices shoot up again. But now the election is over, and Republicans have no reason to worry about anything and nor does Trump. Count on intensifying Iran war after the election, and the oil prices would be higher than what we see now. 

For a change, the trucking industry should not all for a short-lived “immediate relief” mirage. Trump’s real and rich friends own oil  companies, and Trump goal is to make them rich, not give truckers any relief after the election. Only real relief they will get is when Trump’s wild impulses are checked by Democratic majority in Senate and the US Congress .

Home heating oil is nearly identical to diesel fuel, and its price moves in lockstep with the price of diesel.

comments.name: Russ
comments.body:
Here is what will prove to be a universally rejected option.  Double the tax/royalty/excise etc. on diesel then refund it all (plus a little more) back to anyone using it in a commercial venture.  This will provide relief to truckers, famers, fishers , consumers etc. while driving a richly deserved stake in the hearts of the coal-rollers and their ilk.  
I always find it amusing that conservatives(?) always leap to tax cuts as the answer whenever fuel prices (and industry profits) reach point where people may actually cut purchases.  Not an expert on US jurisdictions but here much of the gubbermints portion is fixed per unit sold not price dependent.  They never care when prices are low and the fixed charges are a much bigger part of the total bill though.  The same people. at the same time, lobby for cuts to what big oil pay in taxes as well. comments.body:
I've read about 3 of Barry's Irish novels, picking them randomly at different times from library shelves; discovering only in the middle of one that "Oh, yeah, I've encountered this fictitious family before".

I experienced them as supremely depressing. Probably beyond Beckett; in the realm of N West's "Day of the Locust" and John Barth's early novel "The End of the Road". One of them is about a jolly good fellow who without telling his wife, gambles away the family fortune at the horse races, so that they lose their house....

For decades I did not believe in trigger-warnings; but here I guess I am issuing one: It would be a bad idea for anyone at risk of severe depression, to read these novels.

comments.body: Well done! I haven’t read Sebastian Barry but certainly will after reading this excellent article. This is why the NYT subscription is well worth the money.

comments.name: Stephen
comments.body: Wonderful piece. After reading this, I just ordered a (used) copy of “A Long, Long Way.”

comments.name: Charlotte
comments.body: This article is extraordinary. It skillfully shines a light on the effects of incest on all involved without losing track of their humanity and parallels Barry’s own work, at least as seen by Harvey. It is simultaneously as delicate as lace and as compelling as truth serum. My own life stories share the dance that Barry does between a clear eyed understanding and the fog of doubt. One of the central questions for the child of such a father as Barry and his sister had is, how on earth can I reconcile the deep love and the horror, both of which are forever present in my soul? Harvey’s telling of Barry’s life and writing gives us some guidance.

comments.name: b fagan
comments.body:
"Mr. Milei announced that he would pursue a law allowing the creation of companies whose operations could be carried out by AI agents without human staffing."

So those harmed by the actions, mistakes or unregulated behavior of such companies can directly sue the government of Argentina? Or only sue the particular humans who, behind mazes of corporate hide-and-seek, would be pocketing the money?

Libertarians (the ones who stay so after freshman year in college) are thrilled by a dream that results in complete amnesia as adults. 

Regulations save lives, reduce pollution, punish swindling and theft and financial trickery, and attempt to impose a balance between the possible goods that any business or technology brings against the harms - harms that the people looking to profit will never want to pay for, but instead always seek to push costs onto the public.

Regulations keep libertarians close to the second part of 'freedom' that they so frequently ignore in the real world - 'responsibility'.  Their freedom ends when harms accrue to the rest of the world. If you're not clear on that, picture a libertarian concentrated hog-raising facility.  Uphill from your home in an area prone to heavy rains.

Libertarians ignore that second part and when libertarianism isn't regulated, the harms hit us all.

comments.name: AGI
comments.body:
“‘I kind of pitched them on my craziest idea,’ Mr. Kargieman said in an interview. Argentina, where the work force numbers around 15 million, could have millions of robots producing revenue for the country, he said. With that, he said, Argentina ‘could play a far more important economic role in the world.’”

Given this — being kind here — “thought experiment,” there would need to be a massive fundamental change in the dynamics of the economy. Where would the profits of ”[…] millions of robots producing revenue” go? The factors of production — capital and labor — would be dramatically altered. Capital would retain all economic value and labor would become nearly marginally worthless. Labor would be displaced, and with it, wages. For a functioning economy, consumer demand would somehow need to be sustained.

The two most plausible scenarios —
I.  Further Wealth Concentration and Inequality
Tech oligarchs, their corporations and political cronies, and foreign investors would be the beneficiaries.
II.  Welfare State
Antiquated capitalist classical market mechanisms are supplanted by redistributive policies, such as guaranteed universal incomes, medical, housing, and education, essentially, a social democratic agenda.

In the politics of Argentina today, the faux “libertarian” orthodoxy of Milei’s administration — that includes an influx of U.S. Treasury, IMF, and World Bank subsidies and loans — would portend the former alternative. AI agents cannot be held legally accountable.

comments.name: Rick

When read in conjunction with Ezra Klein's interview of Bill Gates (today's paper), this is terrifying. When it comes to self-control humanity can be counted on having none.

comments.name: La Rana
comments.body: Milei is  growing increasingly unpopular. . A September 2026 survey  put approval of Milei's administration at 42%, with 57% disapproving, and reported deterioration in several measures of political confidence.  Argentines have experienced enough economic “miracle cures” that an outsider saying “this revolutionary technology will transform everything; just get out of the way” is not going to receive automatic acceptance.  Knowing Argentines, this is not going to fly. Though Argentina may be conducting a major political experiment under Milei, it is already growing quite weary,  - and more importantly it does not mean the entire Argentine social contract has been replaced by libertarianism. It hasn’t and it won’t.

comments.name: Eli Hermsen
comments.body: My fear of doing dives and flips off of the diving board haunted me every time I visited the pool when I was younger.

comments.name: Gabe
comments.body: Facing my fear of heights taught me that fear can be overcome if you are willing to challenge yourself. At first, being high up made me nervous especially on like roller coasters but I learned to stay calm and trust myself. This experience showed me that stepping outside my comfort zone -- even when I am scared -- can help me become more confident.

comments.name: Maggie
comments.body: One fear I have not faced yet is the fear of being away from my family for a long time. One step I could take to confront this fear is to spend a little more time away from home. I could prepare myself by staying positive and reminding myself that I can handle it. Both feeling nervous and feeling excited are normal when experiencing something new. If I took this step I think I would become more independent and comfortable being on my own. Beyond that I would learn that being away from people I love doesn’t mean I’m alone.

comments.name: Makenna Grady
comments.body: When I was little, one of my biggest fears with storms and rainy weather. Even if the storm wasn’t that bad, hearing thunder or scenes dark clouds would make me so nervous I wouldn’t even wanna leave the house. As I got older, I started to realize, avoiding storms, would only make the fear worse. I slowly became more comfortable with then as I reminded myself storms were normal. Getting over this fear taught me that that sometimes the things we are most afraid of our actually as scary as we make them seem – our minds can make situations much worse than they really are. Now I’ve learned to appreciate the peacefulness of a big storm. Facing a fear has helped me become more confident showed me how overcoming even a small thing can make a big difference.

comments.name: Sundleen
comments.body: Facing a fear usually starts with overthinking, but actually doing it changes how you see yourself. Last year, I had to present in front of my whole class and spent days stressing that I was going to mess up. But once the day came and I got through it, I realized the stress beforehand was way worse than the actual presentation. Getting through it proved that it was mostly just in my head, beyond that, it showed me I can handle being nervous without completely messing up or blanking out.

comments.name: Jessica Hutauruk
comments.body: Facing a fear can be one of the most difficult things to do. A couple months ago I've always wanted to try out an extracurricular activity. Whether it was a sport, a club, or a community service event. A coach reached out to me and suggested I audition for the Dance Team at my high school. I contemplated if I should try out or not and auditions were just around the corner. Right before auditions, I decided that it was time to try out something new, but personal family issues arose and shifted my final decision. In the end, I realized something else will always "come up" during an important time of my life and I had to try it out. This decision changed my life for the better. I made the team and found a new community of young girls just like me who enjoy dancing, sharing laughter, going on field trips that bring us closer, and having new opportunities. I have gained so much from auditioning for this Dance Team, one of the decisions I will never regret. The friends, memories, and the best experiences I've obtained in my few months on this dance team will be one of the best things I can gain. Being scared for a couple of days to try out something new will never compare to what I've gained today. Only knowing that the path to success is the path with the most resistance.

comments.name: Osme
comments.body: Something that I have learned from facing a fear is that it will forever have an impact on you. Over my junior high years, I struggled with crippling depression and panic attacks which would often times push me to the very edge of the ledge and even though people would often talk me off that ledge-especially the most important people in my life- it was like there was a lingering dark cloud over my head that could not go away. I am now living in an answered prayer that I longed so hard for and sometimes I still struggle with anxiety from time to time-sometimes coming in waves. At the end of the day, the fear I faced will become a testimony that could free somebody and that’s the lasting impact Im choosing to celebrate to triumph over those dark nights.

comments.name: Cole Mocko
comments.body: I used to get terrified whenever I was up in a really tall place with absolutely no support to hold onto. That fear was put to the ultimate test when I visited a skyscraper downtown and faced one of those clear glass ledges that extends out over the city street below. Looking straight down through my own feet at the tiny cars hundreds of feet down made my stomach completely drop—a terrifying moment where it felt like I was floating in mid-air. Even though every instinct told me to step back, I forced myself to walk out onto the transparent tile and look around at the open horizon. Overcoming that paralyzing view taught me a powerful lesson—the boundaries keeping us safe are often much stronger than our anxious minds lead us to believe.

comments.name: stephan morrow
comments.body:
With all the comments and their sometimes conflicting pts of view and sometimes larding it on, IMHO you can't say that there's an equality among artists: some artists break through to new ground and others break the ground. Pollock is undisputably one of those who hammered the earth and changed it. (much to our shame I think it was Life who had an article, somewhat tongue in cheek, that had chimps doing drip paintings.). But if you look at Lee Krasner's 'Rising Green' it's pretty clear that by '72 Krasner had moved on & entered a more hard-edged, minimalist vocabulary which in a way was subtly keeping up with the pressure to move into the minimalist iconography - without losing its Ab Ex history. BTW. It's interesting that only the drip paintings are featured here bec personally, I'm intrigued by the beauty of Pollock's paintings of the late 40's based on Navajo figures and Jungian images. They're all figurative - if out of a dream world (lest we forget that Pollock's father had brought him along to search out Native American cave paintings as a teenager – even though Pollock later became an acolyte of Krishnamurti after attending Hollywood H.S. I say this bec he was a very sophisticated young man & hardly just a farmer's son stumbling into Guggenheim's stable. & his older brother's guidance as well. Finally, by definition a bio pic is always limited just like Frida Kahlo's was – great actors notwithstanding - they don't capture the artist's magic. 
Art Dir
Grt Am Play Series

comments.body:
Something about this exhibition concept makes me uncomfortable.

Krasner was a brilliant, dynamic woman who endured Pollock’s abuse.

She was at the epicenter of the art world of her time, entirely on her own terms. She had a far broader perspective on the art of her time than Pollock did, and framing her in relation to him diminishes her.

She was so much more than her relationship to Pollock.

Why not simply give her her own show at the Met and let us see her in all her glory?

comments.name: JD
comments.body: Pollock's drip paintings hit like a nuclear bomb. But Krasner's art has a developmental arc -- she kept it going. Kind of like the difference between the Sex Pistols -- who made a single monumental album -- and The Clash, whose progression over five albums drew on a much broader swath of styles.

comments.name: Malcolm
comments.body:
I dearly love the Metropolitan Museum. Distance and decrepitude will likely prevent me from visiting this exhibition, but I am very grateful for this account which has increased my appreciation for Lee Krasner.

Might I commend your readership to a recently published book called Vast Horizon, which (among other things) explores the tension between male artists and their artist mates.

comments.name: Jim Fischer
comments.body: I whole-heartedly agree with the writer's friend quoted in the first paragraph.

comments.name: Lynne
comments.body:
Ed Harris directed 2000's "Pollock", a no-holds-barred biopic, delving into the messy (both literally and figuratively), symbiotic relationship between Pollock and Krasner. 

Stephen Holden's reviewed in the NY, here is an excerpt:

'Ed Harris's powerful biographical film ''Pollock'' may be the first movie about a painter to transcend the gushy cliches found in movies that try to unravel the mysteries of artistic creation. It helps, of course, that Jackson Pollock, the Abstract Expressionist giant whom Mr. Harris portrays with a riveting blend of pent-up passion and unleashed physicality, threw his entire body into his work.'

Holden goes so far as to compare Harris to Brando, while deservedly heaping lavish praise on Marcia Gay Harden's portrayal of Krasner:

'In one of the film's most remarkable scenes, she ridicules his suggestion that they have a child with a scalding harangue in which she lists the reasons they shouldn't. Ms. Harden's performance is as uncompromisingly tough as Mr. Harris's. And the pleasure of watching these two superb actors play figures of such stature without a trace of sentimentality is enormous.'

Both actors received Oscar nods for their mesmerizing performances, Harden won the "Best Supporting Actress" award.

The film received mixed reviews. Holden holds that ''Pollock'' is 'for the most part admirable'.

I think Ed Harris is one of the greatest actors of his generation. I think anyone reading this column would be interested in this film.

comments.name: Michael H
comments.body: A great read. It should be noted that in the Artist circles I'm in and through my Art school years decades ago, Lee Krasner and so many female painters were (and are) held in the highest regard. These painters were admired as painters in their own right because the painting held up. I appreciate that this show tries to acknowledge and broaden the impact and talent of Krasner. But I think most painters need no reminding of her greatness and the essential value that female artists have for our understanding the human condition.

I haven't seen a better example of a Slavic language expression that I heard as a child: hočeš nočes moraš.  According to Google: like it or not, you will.  This is the the dictator's motto.  I have absolute power over you and you will obey, or face the consequences.  It's not a negotiation.  It's not win, win.  

Russia and Ukraine are both losing this war.  Ukrainians have proven for years that they will bear any hardship and, not incidentally, invent all manner of creative responses, rather than be under Putin's state gulag.  So Putin demonstrates over and over again that if he can't control you, he will destroy you.  This destruction shows his power.  For a dictator, that works, too.  You can see the ambivalence on his face: ok, I'm not happy with how things are going, but as long as I get to throw bombs, this works.  In the process, he is destroying his own people and country, as well as Ukraine rather than face his own declining power.

comments.name: Ken
comments.body: Use of licence plate readers very well might be a violation of the 4th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution. There is a lawsuit out of Chicago challenging use of such cameras on Constitutional grounds. As I write this, the lawsuit is with the U.S. Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals. It was filed by residents of Cook County, Illinois against the Illinois State Police, Illinois governor and Illinois  Attorney General.

comments.name: Athena
comments.body:
We know that the 4th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution says law enforcement must have reasonable suspicion of a crime and must obtain a search warrant to rummage through private property. There is an underlying principle of RESPECT for private property, and even more fundamentally, the citizen's RIGHT to PRIVACY.

My car is my private property. To search my car, law enforcement needs a warrant. I understand Flock cameras are able to visualize far more than a simple license plate.

Further, the 6th Amendment states that in criminal prosecutions, the accused has the right "to be confronted with the witnesses against him." I have the right to be in the courtroom and SEE the PEOPLE testifying against me. The government cannot convict me using only written statements or hidden witnesses. If the camera is the only witness, how do I confront the camera? I can't: it's not a human being. My lawyer has the right to question the prosecution's witnesses. How does my lawyer converse with a camera? 

The founders fundamentally assumed that ALL LEGAL INTERACTIONS WOULD HAPPEN BETWEEN HUMAN BEINGS. How ever we may have romanticized computers and gadgetry in the 1960s children's cartoon "The Jetsons," we diminish our humanity the more we rely on computers. Read the articles in the Times about how reliance on AI degrades our thinking, or about the unknown danger it poses to our very existence on planet Earth.

A camera is not a person, and therefore fundamentally not a valid a witness.

If a passerby inquired, he would offer one with anchovy or honey. Normally, these would be made inhouse but, in their dream house, my Mom ordered that zeppole, and even fish, had to be cooked outside. As a retired pizza maker, it was my fathers favorite annual tradition! So later, when I lived in Holland, I had to laugh, as well as patronize, the oliebollen (oil ball) stands. comments.name: AB***
comments.body:
Loukoumades, fried Greek honey puffs, were a ritual after Sunday dinner.  Flour, water, sugar, yeast and salt. Let the dough rise, then deep fry the balls until golden. 

It was torture waiting for the dough to rise as we looked forward to devouring dessert, dipped in honey. Even the dog, who did not indulge, sensed the anticipation and was excited for the end product. But how we longed for a shortcut!

After years of making them this way, some "modern" Greek ladies at another church told us their secret. Cut Pillsbury biscuits into quarters. Place into the boiling oil.  

At first, we were skeptical that something so easy would produce a magnificent product like the homemade ones.  Being Greeks, we had to debate for hours if it would work before we actually tried it. 

Once we made the recipe, it tasted the same and saved a lot of time. We were flabbergasted and realized we had to spend more time, not less, in other community churches.  Opa!

comments.body: With all respect to a curator whose career has been truly exceptional, to argue that Ann Temkin has been the sole champion of the fundamental changes at MoMA -the mix of media in the galleries and the overcoming of the archipelago of enclosed islands-departments that MoMA was for many years is a sketchy statement at best, unfair to the truth of history and to many others actors. I was the curator of Latin American Art between 2006 and 2017. Albeit I had the opportunity to work alongside Ann Temkin many times, I cannot fully say that she was a champion of Latin American art. She did not led the initiatives that truly changed the museum structurally, such as the global art publications led by Jay Levenson at the International Program, or the C-MAP curatorial groupings focusing on Latin America, Asia and East of Europe. The true change that is today visible at MoMA should be credited to many others, but most notably to Glenn Lowry and Kathy Halbreich, who took the most radical steps in order to re-conceive the way MoMA offers its displays. I celebrate Ann Temkin's career, but what MoMA is today -great or short of what it could still be- is not to be credited to Ann Temkin's legacy exclusively. If something it is new -and healthy- today at MoMA is that the age of almighty and monumental curators is over. That a woman could have been leading the towering Painting and  Sculpture Department at that pivotal time of enclosure is however a welcoming feat that bear her name.

The Robbed That Smiles

“Ma’am, can you describe the man who robbed the bank?” said Detective Gannon. 

“Yes. I will never forget him. 

“He was a big, tall, short, small guy with sad, smiling eyes and a shock of thin, straight, curly hair. He wore a gray hat, glasses, and sensible shoes. 

“We made small talk — about nothing, really. How we never notice the people we meet every day. Like the plain bank teller who is beautiful in a bland, nondescript way, but who always makes us feel rich — like movie stars.

“I’ll never forget his kind face as he smiled his crooked smile and said, ‘I will always remember you.’ And he handed me five crisp, one-hundred-dollar bills and gallantly walked away. 

“Like I said, I’ll always remember him. I hope that helps, Detective Cannon.”

“Gannon. Have a nice day, ma’am.”

I grew up in a small college town. And took a bus to school. 

And on a fine fall day (coming back home) we'd look out at the campus.  What's all  this?  Why the excitement?  

And when we got off the bus, we smelled something.  

Molasses!  

Certain college kids being tried (in a "kangaroo court") by other college kids.  For various offenses--

--and the guilty were plied with molasses.  And  other substances.  All of them pretty icky.  And it was delightful.  

I say all this to point out the obvious.  That Americans (especially young Americans) take a weird pleasure in--

(1) subjecting people to ritualistic humiliations
(2) being subjected to ritualistic humiliations.  

All in good fun!  Depending on how you define "fun."  But I would point out (in all seriousness)--

--people could die playing around like this.   

That guy doing a 26.2 mile hike.  Consuming huge quantities of hotdogs.  All but immuring himself--

--in a mass of newly acquired flab.  

But looking back on the distant days of my youth--

--I have to admit--

--nobody died during these "kangaroo court" sessions.   And reading this article--

--I find myself murmuring--

--"Let's keep it that way."  

Thanks, Mr. Cacciola.

comments.body:
I visited the villages directly next to the R.A.F. Fairford base a day after dramatic, and still very opaque, scenes unfolded in this quiet corner of the English countryside. Five men were arrested in the early hours of Sunday as part of a counterterrorism investigation after locals spotted a number of masked people and three white vans near the base. The men were released on bail a few hours later, prompting even more confusion.

I'd been here before, a few months earlier, when the U.K. agreed to let the U.S. use the base as part of its war in Iran. At the time, the area around the base was crowded with plane spotters with high-spec zoom lenses hoping to get a glimpse of the U.S. bombers landing and taking off. 

But during this week's visit, the mood was markedly shifted, with 85 households evacuated, armed police surrounding the base, and roadblocks sealing off the tiny village of Whelford, where the man had been arrested. Even as the villagers managed to make their way back home on Monday night, so many questions remained unanswered.

These are unoccupied, need renovation and return to the housing stock and benefit of the local community.  However these units sit idle due to a variety of reasons including overly complicated ownership due to inheritance, owners' lack of funds to renovate, owners reluctant to sell, ownership unknown or not contactable, very low property taxes, owners reluctant to rent long term, etc.  In my community which suffers notably from a lack of long term rental property, over 930 viviendas are unoccupied (18% of the existing stock!) with over 100,000 in the principality of Asturias.  Nationwide, this rate is 14%.  National laws need to be adjusted to encourage the return of these assets to the market.  While not a complete solution, proactively introducing even 10% of these units back into the market would certainly help.

This takes me back to the book Happy Dreams by Jia Pingwa, who writes about a rural migrant worker who moves to the city to earn enough money to marry a decent woman back in his village. Most men from these villages come to the city to build or sustain their families; however, in pursuit of that goal, they take whatever jobs they can find—in this character's case, working as a ragpicker. The book is brilliant and gave me a whole new perspective on Chinese society and what it takes to survive anywhere in the world. Interestingly, Jia was inspired to write this story by the real-life experience of his own friend who moved to town and took up a similar job.

It surprises me how differently we view people and countries until we read their literature. A literary movement centered around the gig economy is especially compelling because we are all so dependent on these workers for the convenience of our daily lives—but at what cost? And if there were not so much discontent, would such works of art ever come to exist?

comments.name: Suzee
comments.body:
I've refused to ever own an Iphone because I knew from the early days of the terrible treatment of Apple's workers in China. They lived in dormitiories 6-10 per room and worked very long hours 6 days a week for low wages until the Chinese govt stepped in and demanded higher wages.   Yet the Apple owners sold their phones for very large $s despite the low cost of producing the phones.  I believe the situation is much the same for industrial workers in several other Asian countries, not only China.  

However, those Chinese country workers are still better off financially than if they'd remained in their home villages, where there was no work for them. They migrate to the large cities to gain an income for their families.

The Chinese economy is going downhill but the situation is the same in most nations.  BUT Chinese cities are so vibrant, huge and beautiful. China has a larger percentage of unemployed university educated young people than ever before, especially in the major cities, because of their advanced technology and population. However many of those ex-uni students are brilliant at STEM subjects and gain great jobs.

Despite many bad things that regularly get reported about the Chinese govt., I have enjoyed lengthy periods of time in Beijing and Shanghai, as well as travelling the country with only 2 other Australians each time without guides. I found it a very safe country to walk in, even at night when I was on my own.

comments.name: P. Callil
comments.body:
Let’s face it, the gig economy is bleak and disastrous for all low paid workers. Whether it’s Ali Baba or Amazon, it appears to make little difference.  I keep reading in the NYT about how bad the economy in China is.  I’ve just spent three weeks in China and it’s an amazing place - sparkling clean, grand in scale, welcoming and above all, safe. The food is incredible. It’s bustling and busy and an utter contrast to the inequality, violence and homelessness that characterises the myriad of US cities visited over the last 40 years. 

While Trump America yearns for an illusory past, China is the future. It was almost impossible to see anything here that marked this as a communist country.  Do I trust the Chinese government? Absolutely not.  Do I now trust the American government after what Trump has deliberately done? Absolutely not.  The gap between rich and poor grows day by day in America. The gig economy is awful for workers but singling out China for this is hardly the full picture unless of course, there is just part of an ongoing narrative of how bad the Chinese economy is.

comments.name: N.G. Krishnan
comments.body:
The New York Times deserves immense credit for shining a spotlight on China's worker-poets—a crucial public service at a time when few outlets examine the human cost behind global manufacturing.

That factory workers must turn to verse to preserve their dignity reveals a tragic irony: a state founded on Marxist liberation now functions as a high-tech engine of labor exploitation. Aeons away from the promise of worker solidarity, the regime has fused absolute authority with market capitalism, turning the party into the ultimate parasitic force.

This is another grim chapter in The God That Failed and a stark reminder of the immortality of George Orwell’s Animal Farm. As Arthur Koestler, Ignazio Silone, and Orwell recognized mid-century, no theory—no matter how rosy on paper—can overcome the flaws of human nature. 

When absolute power is granted to a revolutionary, the pigs inevitably walk on two legs.

I live alone and I already have to throw away a lot of vegetables just trying to eat a few different ones because I need a fraction of what I buy and the rest I can't use. I use less than half a head of purple cabbage even putting it on multiple salads and other meals, I have never used up an entire container of arugula, etc. Grapes are another one, lettuces, all those kind of things. I can't buy a 1/4 pound of broccoli or a few leaves of kale. And a lot of the "cheaper" options like Aldi or Costco aren't really cheaper for me because they come in bulk. comments.name: susan gioia
comments.body: My 67 year old brother was diagnosed with FTD (also primary progressive aphasia) four years ago at age 63. He is now in a subacute facility after a hospital stay for seizures- which began last April. His latest diagnosis two years agowas Alzheimers which came after a PET scan. His wife has proxy and cannot take care of him at home, though my sister and I often wonder if that could be doable as we feel he would be happier at home with one or two aides as his main difficulty is communication. She visits him at least four times a week, we are 90 minutes away and visit once a week. It's been an increasingly stressful situation for her the last four years with him living at home until this past spring, so we understand why he can't live at home. If we had proxy we would try to bring him to take care of him, though I know it might not work out. The thing that stood out to me in this article is that the woman, Barb, is not following up on the DNA results- hereditary or sporadic? I understand that the best way in our case would be for my brother to have a noninvasive swab test taken, but his wife and children (who also have children) say they want this, but are not acting on it. So it is all, as the article states, very hard on families, but mostly on my beautiful younger brother who was just on the verge of retirement with young grandchildren. Besides praising this article, I look forward to reading other readers' comments as so much can be learned from each other.

comments.name: Mihailo Zoin
comments.body:
Progress or Regress?

Viewed through a modern lens, the verdict is striking: we have skyrocketed technologically, but stagnated morally.

Technological Progress: In 1988, America held its breath just to put Discovery safely back into orbit; today, reusable private rockets land on floating platforms. Willie Mays' breathtaking 1954 catch is now instantly quantified by high-speed spatial tracking and launch-angle metrics.   

Ethical & Geopolitical Regress: Zola’s lonely battle against systemic prejudice and smear campaigns has merely migrated from print to algorithmic mob rule and weaponized deepfakes. Meanwhile, the 1911 war over North African soil and the 1941 atrocities in Babyn Yar are grim reminders that modern borders and ethnic hatreds still bleed across the exact same geography.
